title: Document Automation (PDFs, Invoices, and E-signatures)
summary: A large chunk of business work revolves around documents - invoices, contracts, reports, certificates - and automating their creation and processing is a high-value, very common request, so document automation is a practical skill that quickly pays o
content:
# Document Automation (PDFs, Invoices, and E-signatures) ##### Twenty-two invoices, every Friday A design studio in Kochi had a Friday ritual. The office manager opened an invoice template in Word, changed the client name, the project description, the line items and the amount, exported it as a PDF, renamed the file, attached it to an email, wrote a covering note, sent it, and logged the number and amount in a spreadsheet. Twenty-two times. Three and a half hours. Every week. With occasional errors that were genuinely expensive — an invoice sent to the wrong client, a duplicated invoice number that confused their accountant for a month. Documents are where business processes become physical. Invoices, contracts, certificates, offer letters, reports, quotations — every one of them is a template plus data plus a delivery step, which is to say, every one of them is an automation waiting to be built. This is high-value, very billable work, and the underlying pattern is simpler than it looks. ##### The two halves of document automation Everything in this field is one of two operations, and the assignment asks you to distinguish them clearly. **Generation** — *structured data → document*. You have clean data (an order record) and you produce a formatted PDF. This direction is deterministic and reliable: you control the template, so you know exactly what comes out. Invoice creation, contract generation, certificate issuing. **Extraction** — *document → structured data*. You receive a PDF (a supplier invoice, a signed form, a bank statement) and need to pull values out of it. This direction is *hard*, because you did not create the document and every supplier formats theirs differently. Accounts-payable processing, receipt capture, form digitization. The asymmetry is important: generation is a solved problem you can automate with confidence today, while extraction is a probabilistic problem requiring validation and, often, human review. ##### Generating PDFs from templates Four approaches, in ascending order of control: **1. Google Docs as a template engine.** The most accessible route, and it works beautifully. Create a Doc with placeholders like `{{customer_name}}` and `{{total}}`, then in your automation: copy the template file, replace the placeholders with real values, export as PDF. Zapier, Make and n8n all have Google Docs nodes with a "Create document from template" action. **2. Dedicated document services** — DocuPilot, PDFMonkey, Documint, Carbone. You design a template in their editor, POST JSON to their API, and receive a PDF URL. They handle pagination, page breaks, repeating line-item tables and fonts — the fiddly parts. Worth the small monthly cost for anything client-facing. **3. HTML to PDF.** Design the document as an HTML page with CSS, then render it. This gives you full control over layout and is what most SaaS products do internally. Libraries: WeasyPrint or wkhtmltopdf in Python, Puppeteer/Playwright in JavaScript, or hosted APIs like PDFShift. **4. Programmatic generation** in code with ReportLab (Python) or PDFKit. Maximum control, most effort. Use when you need precise positioning or dynamic complexity. Here is approach 3 in Python, which shows the whole pattern clearly: ```python from datetime import date from jinja2 import Template from weasyprint import HTML TEMPLATE = Template("""

INVOICE

{{ invoice_no }} · {{ issue_date }}

Bill to:
{{ customer.name }}
{{ customer.company }}
{{ customer.address }}

{% for it in items %} {% endfor %}
DescriptionQty RateAmount
{{ it.description }} {{ it.qty }} {{ "%.2f"|format(it.rate) }} {{ "%.2f"|format(it.qty * it.rate) }}
Subtotal {{ "%.2f"|format(subtotal) }}
GST @ 18% {{ "%.2f"|format(gst) }}
Total (INR) {{ "%.2f"|format(total) }}
""") items = [ {"description": "Brand identity design", "qty": 1, "rate": 45000.00}, {"description": "Landing page (3 pages)", "qty": 3, "rate": 8500.00}, ] subtotal = sum(i["qty"] * i["rate"] for i in items) gst = round(subtotal * 0.18, 2) html = TEMPLATE.render( invoice_no="INV-2026-0412", issue_date=date.today().strftime("%d %b %Y"), customer={"name": "Ananya Rao", "company": "Northwind Logistics", "address": "42 Baner Road, Pune 411045"}, items=items, subtotal=subtotal, gst=gst, total=subtotal + gst, ) HTML(string=html).write_pdf("INV-2026-0412.pdf") print("Generated INV-2026-0412.pdf") ``` Note that the totals are computed **in code, not by the template and never by an AI**. Arithmetic on money must be deterministic. ##### Extracting data from PDFs and OCR basics Extraction starts with a question: **is this PDF text-based or image-based?** A **text-based PDF** was generated digitally and contains actual selectable text. You can extract it directly and reliably: ```python import pdfplumber with pdfplumber.open("supplier-invoice.pdf") as pdf: text = "\n".join(page.extract_text() or "" for page in pdf.pages) tables = pdf.pages[0].extract_tables() # often the real prize ``` An **image-based PDF** is a scan or a photograph — a picture of a page with no text layer. Selecting text in your PDF viewer tells you instantly: if nothing highlights, it is an image. That is when you need **OCR (Optical Character Recognition)** — software that recognizes characters in an image. **Tesseract** is the open-source standard (Ray Smith's overview paper describes its architecture), and cloud services like Google Document AI, AWS Textract and Azure Form Recognizer offer higher accuracy plus layout understanding. ```python import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path pages = convert_from_path("scanned-invoice.pdf", dpi=300) # 300 dpi matters text = "\n".join(pytesseract.image_to_string(p, lang="eng") for p in pages) ``` OCR quality depends heavily on input quality: 300 dpi or better, straight (deskewed), good contrast, clean scan. A phone photo taken at an angle in poor light will produce garbage, and no amount of post-processing fixes it. **Where AI transforms this.** Classic extraction uses regex or fixed coordinates: "the invoice number is after the words 'Invoice No'." That works until a supplier redesigns their template, at which point it silently breaks. Modern **vision-capable LLMs** can take the page image or OCR text and return structured JSON regardless of layout: ```text Prompt: "Extract from this invoice. Return ONLY JSON: { invoice_number, invoice_date (ISO), supplier_name, currency, line_items:[{description, qty, unit_price, amount}], subtotal, tax, total, confidence } If a field is not present, use null. Do not calculate missing values." ``` This handles 200 supplier formats with one prompt — a genuine step change for accounts-payable automation. The caveats from AI day all apply, doubled: **validate everything**. Check that line items sum to the subtotal, that the total equals subtotal plus tax, that the date parses, that the invoice number is not a duplicate. Route anything failing validation, or with low confidence, to a human. Never let an LLM's arithmetic be the final word on a payment amount. ##### E-signature integration For contracts, offer letters and agreements, generation is only half the job — you need a legally valid signature. **DocuSign**, **Adobe Sign**, **Dropbox Sign** and **Zoho Sign** all provide APIs, and India's IT Act recognizes electronic signatures under defined conditions. The API flow, using DocuSign as the model: 1. **Create an envelope** — the container holding your document(s). 2. **Add recipients** with roles (signer, approver, carbon copy) and a **routing order** if signatures must happen in sequence. 3. **Place tabs** — the signature, initial, date and text fields, positioned either by coordinates or by **anchor strings** (invisible markers like `/sig1/` in your document text). Anchors are far more robust because they move with the content. 4. **Send.** Recipients get an email and sign in a browser. 5. **Receive webhooks** (DocuSign Connect) for events: `sent`, `delivered`, `completed`, `declined`, `voided`. 6. **On completion**, download the signed PDF plus the **certificate of completion** — an audit document recording signer identity, IP addresses and timestamps, which is what gives the signature its evidentiary weight. Design the workflow around the webhook, not around polling, and always store both the signed document and the certificate. ##### The full invoice pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Order recorded] --> B[Get next invoice number
atomic DB sequence] B --> C[Compute totals in code
subtotal, GST, total] C --> D[Render template → PDF] D --> E[Save to Drive
Invoices/2026/03/] E --> F[Email PDF to customer] F --> G[Log to database
number, amount, file URL, status] G --> H{Needs signature?} H -->|yes| I[Create e-sign envelope] I --> J[Webhook: completed →
store signed PDF + certificate] H -->|no| K[Done] ``` The **invoice number** step deserves attention. Numbers must be unique, sequential and gapless for accounting and GST compliance. Generating them from a timestamp or a spreadsheet row count creates duplicates under concurrency. Use a database sequence or an atomic counter — `INSERT ... RETURNING` on a table with a `BIGSERIAL` gives you correctness for free. ##### Common pitfalls - **Computing money in the template or with AI.** Do it in code, with `NUMERIC`/decimal types. - **Non-atomic invoice numbering** producing duplicates. - **Overwriting files** because two documents got the same name. Include the invoice number and date. - **Assuming every PDF has a text layer** — check, and fall back to OCR. - **Low-resolution OCR input** — 300 dpi minimum, deskew first. - **Regex extraction tied to one supplier's layout** breaking silently on a redesign. - **No validation of extracted values** before paying an invoice. - **Emailing the wrong PDF** — verify the attachment matches the recipient before sending, especially in loops. - **Storing signed contracts without the completion certificate.** - **Ignoring retention and privacy** — invoices and contracts contain personal and financial data. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build an automation that takes data from a form or sheet, **generates a personalized PDF from a template**, emails it to the recipient, and **saves a copy to Drive**. The Google Docs template route is the fastest way to a working result; use `{{placeholder}}` markers and a "create document from template" step. The mini project is the studio's Friday afternoon, automated: an **end-to-end invoice automation** where a recorded order generates a branded invoice PDF with the order details, emails it to the customer, saves it to a **dated folder**, and logs the invoice number and amount to a **database**. Get the numbering right — a sequence, not a counter — and compute totals in code. Then, as a write-up, calculate the hours saved per month. That number is what sells the work. For the assignment, explain **generation versus extraction** and why the second is harder, describe **when OCR is needed** (image-based PDFs and scans, identified by the absence of a text layer), and outline **how AI improves extraction from messy PDFs** — layout-independent structured output from vision models, with mandatory validation of arithmetic and a human-review path for low confidence. ##### Key takeaways - Document automation splits into generation (data → document, deterministic and reliable) and extraction (document → data, probabilistic and needing validation). - Generate PDFs from Google Docs templates, dedicated services, or HTML+CSS rendering — and always compute money in code, never in the template. - Text-based PDFs can be parsed directly; scans require OCR at 300 dpi, and vision-capable LLMs now handle varied layouts far better than regex. - E-signature APIs work as envelopes with recipients, anchor-based tabs and completion webhooks — always store the signed file *and* the certificate of completion. - Get invoice numbering atomic and unique, name files predictably, validate extracted values before acting, and treat documents as the sensitive data they are.
